{{Short description|Unreproducible object used in digital security}}
{{context|date=February 2016}}
In [[computing]] and [[cryptography]], a '''physical unclonable function''' or '''PUF''' is a physical object whose operation cannot be reproduced ("cloned") in a physical way (by making another system using the same technology), such that for a given input and conditions (challenge), provides a physically defined "digital fingerprint"<ref name="maes2013">{{Citation |last=Maes |first=Roel |chapter=Physically Unclonable Functions: Properties |date=2013 |title=Physically Unclonable Functions |pages=49–80 |place=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-41395-7_3 |isbn=978-3-642-41394-0}}</ref> output (response) that serves as a [[unique identifier]]—most often for a semiconductor device such as a microprocessor or a material producing an optical signal. PUFs are often based on unique physical variations occurring naturally during semiconductor manufacturing.<ref name="ieeexplore.ieee.org">{{Cite journal |last1=Kamal |first1=Kamal Y. |last2=Muresan |first2=Radu |date=2019 |title=Mixed-Signal Physically Unclonable Function With CMOS Capacitive Cells |journal=IEEE Access |volume=7 |pages=130977–130998 |doi=10.1109/ACCESS.2019.2938729  |doi-access=free|bibcode=2019IEEEA...7m0977K |s2cid=202766809 |issn=2169-3536|hdl=10214/17525 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> 

A PUF is a physical entity embodied in a physical structure. PUFs can be implemented in [[integrated circuits]], including [[Field-programmable gate array|FPGAs]],<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Nozaki |first1=Yusuke |last2=Yoshikawa |first2=Masaya |title=2019 Cybersecurity and Cyberforensics Conference (CCC) |chapter=Countermeasure of Lightweight Physical Unclonable Function Against Side-Channel Attack |date=May 2019 |location=Melbourne, Australia |publisher=IEEE |pages=30–34 |doi=10.1109/CCC.2019.00-13 |isbn=978-1-7281-2600-5|s2cid=203655491 }}</ref> and can be used in applications with high-security requirements, more specifically [[cryptography]], [[Internet of things|Internet of things (IOT)]] devices<ref>{{Cite thesis |last=Josiah |first=J. G. |date=2020 |title=The CCAP: A New Physical Unclonable Function (PUF) for Protecting Internet of Things (IoT) and Other FPGA-based Embedded Systems |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/2406630562 |journal=ProQuest|type=Ph.D |id={{ProQuest|2406630562}} }}</ref> and [[Privacy and blockchain|privacy]] protection.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Lipps |first1=Christoph |last2=Mallikarjun |first2=Sachinkumar Bavikatti |last3=Strufe |first3=Matthias |last4=Heinz |first4=Christopher |last5=Grimm |first5=Christoph |last6=Schotten |first6=Hans Dieter |title=2020 3rd International Conference on Data Intelligence and Security (ICDIS) |chapter=Keep Private Networks Private: Secure Channel-PUFs, and Physical Layer Security by Linear Regression Enhanced Channel Profiles |date=June 2020 |pages=93–100 |publisher=IEEE |doi=10.1109/icdis50059.2020.00019|isbn=978-1-7281-9379-3 |s2cid=231683963 }}</ref> The term is also commonly expanded as a '''physically unclonable function''' in the academic literature.<ref name="maes2013" />

==History==
Early references about systems that exploit the physical properties of disordered systems for authentication purposes date back to Bauder in 1983<ref>D.W. Bauder, "An anti-counterfeiting concept for currency systems," Research report PTK-11990. Sandia National Labs. Albuquerque, NM, 1983.</ref> and Simmons in 1984.<ref>G. Simmons, "A system for verifying user identity and authorization at the point-of-sale or access," Cryptologia, vol. 8, no. 1, pp. 1–21, 1984.</ref><ref>G. Simmons, "Identification of data, devices, documents, and individuals," in IEEE International Carnahan Conference on Security Technology, 1991, pp. 197–218.</ref> Naccache and Frémanteau provided an authentication scheme in 1992 for memory cards.<ref>David Naccache and Patrice Frémanteau, Unforgeable identification device, identification device reader and method of identification, August 1992.[http://v3.espacenet.com/publicationDetails/biblio?DB=EPODOC&adjacent=true&locale=en_gb&FT=D&date=19940223&CC=EP&NR=0583709A1&KC=A1]{{Dead link|date=February 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref>  PUFs were first formally proposed in a general fashion by Pappu in 2001,<ref name=":1">{{cite journal | last1 = Pappu | first1 = R. | last2 = Recht | first2 = B. | last3 = Taylor | first3 = J. | last4 = Gershenfeld | first4 = N. | year = 2002| title = Physical one-way functions | journal = Science | volume = 297 | issue = 5589| pages = 2026–2030 | doi = 10.1126/science.1074376 | pmid = 12242435 | bibcode = 2002Sci...297.2026P | hdl = 1721.1/45499 | url = https://nbviewer.jupyter.org/github/rpappu/pdf-publications/blob/master/Pappu-Science-2002.pdf | hdl-access = free }}</ref> under the name ''physical one-way function'' (POWF), with the term PUF being coined in 2002,<ref name="ReferenceA">Blaise Gassend, Dwaine Clarke, Marten van Dijk and Srinivas Devadas. Silicon Physical Random Functions. Proceedings of the Computer and Communications Security Conference, November 2002</ref> whilst describing the first ''integrated'' PUF where, unlike PUFs based on optics, the measurement circuitry and the PUF are integrated onto the same electrical circuit (and fabricated on silicon).

Starting in 2010, PUF gained attention in the [[smartcard]] market as a promising way to provide "silicon fingerprints", creating cryptographic keys that are unique to individual smartcards.<ref>{{cite web | last = Clarke | first = Peter | title = London Calling: Security technology takes time | newspaper = EE Times | publisher = UBM Tech Electronics | date = 22 February 2013 | url = http://www.eetimes.com/author.asp?section_id=36&doc_id=1287041 | access-date = 1 July 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite news | title = NXP and Intrinsic-ID to raise smart chip security | newspaper = EE Times | publisher = UBM Tech Electronics | date = 21 January 2010 | url = http://www.eetimes.com/document.asp?doc_id=1254886 | access-date = 1 July 2013}}</ref>

PUFs are now established as a secure alternative to battery-backed storage of secret keys in commercial [[FPGA]]s, such as the [[Xilinx]] Zynq Ultrascale+,<ref>[https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/xilinx-addresses-rigorous-security-demands-at-fifth-annual-working-group-for-broad-range-of-applications-300351291.html Xilinx Addresses Rigorous Security Demands at Fifth Annual Working Group for Broad Range of Applications]</ref> and Altera Stratix 10.<ref>[https://www.intrinsic-id.com/altera-reveals-stratix-10-with-intrinsic-ids-puf-technology/ intrinsic-id.com]</ref>

==Concept==
PUFs depend on the uniqueness of their physical microstructure. This microstructure depends on random physical factors introduced during manufacturing. These factors are unpredictable and uncontrollable, which makes it virtually impossible to duplicate or clone the structure.

Rather than embodying a single cryptographic key, PUFs implement [[challenge–response authentication]] to evaluate this microstructure. When a physical stimulus is applied to the structure, it reacts in an unpredictable (but repeatable) way due to the complex interaction of the stimulus with the physical microstructure of the device. This exact microstructure depends on physical factors introduced during manufacture, which are unpredictable  (like a [[fair coin]]). The applied stimulus is called the challenge, and the reaction of the PUF is called the response. A specific challenge and its corresponding response together form a challenge-response pair or CRP. The device's identity is established by the properties of the microstructure itself.  As this structure is not directly revealed by the challenge-response mechanism, such a device is resistant to [[spoofing attack]]s.

Using a [[fuzzy extractor]] or the fuzzy [[commitment scheme]] that are provably suboptimal in terms of storage and privacy leakage amount or using nested [[Polar code (coding theory)|polar codes]]<ref name="gunluwz"/> that can be made asymptotically optimal, one can extract a unique strong cryptographic key from the physical microstructure.<ref name="Tuyls2007">{{cite book |last1=Tuyls |first1=Pim |last2=Škorić |first2=Boris |last3=Kevenaar |first3=Tom | doi = 10.1007/978-1-84628-984-2 | title=Security with Noisy Data: Private Biometics, Secure Key Storage and Anti-counterfeiting | year=2007 | publisher=Springer | isbn=978-184628-983-5}}</ref> The same [[unique key]] is reconstructed every time the PUF is evaluated.<ref name="Maes2013">{{cite book |last1=Maes |first1=R. |title=Physically unclonable functions: Constructions, Properties and Applications |date=2013 |publisher=Springer | isbn=978-3-642-41395-7}}</ref><ref>
[https://www.maximintegrated.com/en/design/partners-and-technology/design-technology/chipdna-puf-technology.html "PUF Technology Overview"].
</ref>
The challenge-response mechanism is then implemented using [[cryptography]]. {{Citation needed|reason=this seems to contradict the previous paragraph that says 'Rather than embodying a single cryptographic key, PUFs implement challenge-response authentication to evaluate this microstructure.'|date=October 2018}}

PUFs can be implemented with a very small hardware investment compared to other cryptographic primitives that provide unpredictable input/output behavior, such as [[Pseudorandom function family|pseudo-random functions]]. In some cases, PUFs can even be built from existing hardware with the right properties.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Journal of Electrical and Electronics Research (JEER) |url=https://www.academicedgepress.co.uk/JEER?ArticleID=20 |access-date=2026-07-22 |website=www.academicedgepress.co.uk |language=en}}</ref>

Unclonability means that each PUF device has a unique and unpredictable way of mapping challenges to responses, even if it was manufactured with the same process as a similar device, and it is infeasible to construct a PUF with the same challenge-response behavior as another given PUF because exact control over the manufacturing process is infeasible. Mathematical unclonability means that it should be very hard to compute an unknown response given the other CRPs or some of the properties of the random components from a PUF. This is because a response is created by a complex interaction of the challenge with many or all of the random components. In other words, given the design of the PUF system, without knowing ''all'' of the physical properties of the random components, the CRPs are highly unpredictable. The combination of physical and mathematical unclonability renders a PUF truly unclonable.<ref name="Maes2013"/><ref>C. Herder, L. Ren, M. van Dijk, M-D. Yu, and S. Devadas, "Trapdoor Computational Fuzzy Extractors and Cryptographically-Secure Physical Unclonable Functions," IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing, January 2017.</ref>

Note that a PUF is "unclonable" using the same physical implementation, but once a PUF key is extracted, there's generally no problem with cloning the key – the output of the PUF – using other means. For ''extensive PUFs'', defined later, in some cases one can train a [[neural network]] on observed challenge-response pairs and use it to predict unobserved responses - however this can have a limited effect depending on the strength and unpredictability of the PUF.<ref>A. Vijayakumar, V. C. Patil, C. B. Prado, and S. Kundu, "Machine learning resistant strong PUF: Possible or a pipe dream?," 2016 IEEE International Symposium on Hardware Oriented Security and Trust (HOST), 2016.</ref>

Because of these properties, PUFs can be used as a unique and untamperable device identifier. PUFs can also be used for secure [[key generation]] and storage and for a source of [[randomness]].{{Citation needed|reason=this seems to directly contradict the statement above 'Note that a PUF is "unclonable" using the same physical implementation, but once a PUF key is extracted, there's generally no problem with cloning the key – the output of the PUF – using other means.'|date=May 2026}}

==Classification==
{{Unreferenced section|date=July 2026}}

===Extensive / confined (strong / weak)===
* ''Strong / weak'' PUF terms are deprecated, because the term 'Weak PUF' does not properly describe the property of the PUF; ISO/IEC 20897 defines PUF terms as ''extensive PUF'', ''confined PUF''.
* ''Confined'' PUFs can be considered a kind of memory that is randomly initialized during PUF manufacture. A challenge can be considered an address within the memory, and response can be considered the random value stored by that address. This way count of unique challenge-response pairs (CRPs) scales lineary with count of random elements of the PUF. The advantage of such PUFs is that they are actual [[random oracle]]s, so are immune to machine-learning attacks. The weakness is that count of CRPs is small and can be exhausted either by an adversary, that can probe the PUF directly, or during authentication protocols over insecure channels, in which case verifier has to keep track of challenges already known to adversary. That's why the main application of confined PUFs is the source of randomness for deriving crypto keys.
* ''Extensive'' PUFs are systems doing computation based on their internal structure. Their count of unique CRPs scales faster than linearily with increase in count of random elements because of interactions between the elements. The advantage is that this way space of CRPs can be made large enough to make its exhaustion practically impossible and collisions of 2 randomly chosen elements of the space improbable enough, allowing the verifying party not to keep track of used elements but just to choose them randomly from the space. Another advantage is that the randomness can be stored not only within the elements but also within their interactions, which sometimes can not be read directly. The weakness is that the same elements and their interactions are reused for different challenges, which opens the possibility to derive some information about the elements and their connections and use it to predict the reaction of the system to the unobserved challenges.

=== Implicit / explicit ===
All implementations of a certain PUF within certain device are created uniformly using scalable processes. For example when a cryptoprocessor based on a silicon chip is produced, a lot of processors are created on the same silicon wafer. Foundry equipment applies the same operations to all the chips on a wafer and tries to do it as much reproducible as possible in order to have predictable and high performance and reliability characteristics within all the chips. Despite this there should be generated randomness to make PUF in each chip unique.

* ''Explicit'' PUF randomness is created explicitly in a separate technological operation. It is a disadvantage because a separate operation imposes additional costs and because manufacturer can intentionally replace that separate operation with something else, which can reduce randomness and compromise security characteristics.
* ''Implicit'' PUF uses technology imperfections as a source of randomness by designing a PUF as a device which operation is strongly affected by technology imperfections instead of being unaffected, as it is done for usual circuitry, and fabricating it simultaneously with the rest of the device. Since foundries themselves cannot defeat the imperfections of the technology despite having strong economic incentive in being capable to fabricate more performant and more reliable chips, it gives some protection from foundry backdooring such PUFs this way. Backdooring PUFs by tampering with lithographic masks can be detected by [[reverse engineering]] the resulting devices. Fabricating the PUF as the part of the rest of the device makes it cheaper than explicit PUFs.

=== Intrinsic / extrinsic ===
* ''Extrinsic'' PUFs rely on sensors to measure a system containing the randomness. Such sensors are a weak point since they can be replaced with fakes sending the needed measurements.
* ''Intrinsic'' PUF operation is affected by randomness contained within the system itself.

==Types==
{{Main|Types of physical unclonable function}}

Over 40 types of PUF have been suggested.<ref name=McGrath2019>{{cite journal |last1=McGrath |first1=Thomas |last2=Bagci |first2=Ibrahim E. |last3=Wang |first3=Zhiming M. |last4=Roedig |first4=Utz |last5=Young |first5=Robert J. |title=A PUF taxonomy |journal=Applied Physics Reviews |date=2019 |volume=6 |issue=11303 |page=011303 |doi=10.1063/1.5079407 |bibcode=2019ApPRv...6a1303M |doi-access=free }}</ref> These range from PUFs that evaluate an intrinsic element of a pre-existing [[Integrated circuit|integrated electronic]] system<ref name=Helinski2009>{{cite book |last1=Helinski |first1=R. |last2=Acharyya |first2=D. |last3=Plusquellic |first3=J. |title=Proceedings of the 46th Annual Design Automation Conference |chapter=A physical unclonable function defined using power distribution system equivalent resistance variations |date=2009 |pages=676–681|doi=10.1145/1629911.1630089 |isbn=978-1-60558-497-3 |s2cid=2537549 }}</ref> to concepts that involve explicitly introducing random particle distributions to the surface of physical objects for authentication.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chong |first1=C. N. |last2=Jiang |first2=J. |last3=Guo |first3=L. |title=Anti-counterfeiting with a random pattern |journal=Proceedings of Second International Conference on Emerging Security Information, Systems and Technologies (SECURWARE) |date=2008 |pages=146–153}}</ref> All PUFs are subject to environmental variations such as temperature, supply voltage and [[electromagnetic interference]], which can affect their performance. Therefore, rather than just being random, the real power of a PUF is its ability to be different between devices but simultaneously to be the same under different environmental conditions on the same device.

=== Fractional Hamming distance (fHD) ===

The fractional [[Hamming distance]] (fHD) is a commonly used metric to quantify the difference between two binary responses.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=T. |last2=Shu |first2=Z. |last3=Zhang |first3=L. |last4=Chen |first4=Y. |last5=Feng |first5=Z. |last6=Hu |first6=Y. |last7=Huang |first7=F. |last8=Wang |first8=P. |last9=Li |first9=D. |last10=Yao |first10=Y. |year=2021 |title=Random nanofracture-enabled physical unclonable function |journal=Advanced Materials Technologies |volume=6 |issue=6 |doi=10.1002/admt.202001073 |article-number=2001073}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Esidir |first1=A. |last2=Kiremitler |first2=N. B. |last3=Kalay |first3=M. |last4=Basturk |first4=A. |last5=Onses |first5=M. S. |year=2022 |title=Unclonable features via electrospraying of bulk polymers |journal=ACS Applied Polymer Materials |volume=4 |issue=8 |pages=5952–5964 |bibcode=2022AAPM....4.5952E |doi=10.1021/acsapm.2c00803 |doi-access=free}}</ref> It is defined as:

<math>
fHD(A,B) = \frac{1}{ab} \sum_{I=1}^{a} \sum_{J=1}^{b} (A \oplus B)_{IJ}
</math>

where ''A'' and ''B'' are binary arrays representing two responses, ''a'' and ''b'' are the dimensions of these arrays, and ⊕ denotes the bitwise XOR operation. The summation is carried out over all pixel positions ''I'' (1, 2, ..., ''a'') and ''J'' (1, 2, ..., ''b'') in the arrays. The result gives a normalized measure of similarity between the two arrays, ranging from 0 (identical) to 1 (completely different).

In practice, the fHD is often applied to sets of responses. For example, in intra-PUF reliability analysis, the fHD is calculated across repeated measurements (the 'C' set), and the mean value of the fHD is reported as the reliability value.

=== Uniqueness ===

Uniqueness is a measure of how distinguishable the responses of different PUF instances are. It is typically quantified by the mean of the inter-device fractional Hamming distances (inter-fHD). Uniqueness is commonly used in the literature.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Esidir |first1=A. |last2=Kayaci |first2=N. |last3=Kiremitler |first3=N. B. |last4=Kalay |first4=M. |last5=Sahin |first5=F. |last6=Sezer |first6=G. |last7=Kaya |first7=M. |last8=Onses |first8=M. S. |year=2023 |title=Food-grade physically unclonable functions |journal=ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces |volume=15 |issue=35 |pages=41373–41384 |bibcode=2023AAMI...1541373E |doi=10.1021/acsami.3c09035 |pmc=10485800 |pmid=37615185}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kayaci |first1=N. |last2=Ozdemir |first2=R. |last3=Kalay |first3=M. |last4=Kiremitler |first4=N. B. |last5=Usta |first5=H. |last6=Onses |first6=M. S. |year=2022 |title=Organic light-emitting physically unclonable functions |journal=Advanced Functional Materials |volume=32 |issue=14 |doi=10.1002/adfm.202108675 |article-number=2108675 |bibcode=2022AdvFM..3208675K }}</ref> This is given by:

<math>
\mu_{2} = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{2}} \sum_{x=1}^{N-1} \sum_{y=x+1}^{N} fHD(D_{x}, D_{y})
</math>

where ''μ<sub>2</sub>'' is the inter-fHD mean, ''N'' is the number of inter-device responses, and ''D<sub>x</sub>'' and ''D<sub>y</sub>'' are arrays from the inter-device set {''D''}. Thus, ''N'' is also the total number of arrays in the set {''D''}.<<ref name=":2">{{cite journal |last1=Maiti |first1=A. |last2=Kim |first2=I. |last3=Schaumont |first3=P. |year=2012 |title=A robust physical unclonable function with enhanced challenge-response set |journal=IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security |volume=7 |issue=1 |pages=333–345 |bibcode=2012ITIF....7..333M |doi=10.1109/TIFS.2011.2165540}}</ref>

The parameter commonly reported as "uniqueness" is then expressed as:

<math>
Uniqueness = \mu_{2} \times 100\%
</math>

The ideal value for ''μ<sub>2</sub>'' is 0.5. This indicates that, on average, different PUF instances produce responses that differ in 50% of their bits, demonstrating both randomness and uniqueness.

=== Reliability ===

Reliability, commonly reported alongside uniformity, is a measure of the consistency of a PUF's responses when the same challenge is applied multiple times. It is quantified by the mean intra-device fractional Hamming distance (intra-fHD), expressed as:

<math>
\mu_{1} = \frac{1}{\binom{N}{2}} \sum_{x=1}^{N-1} \sum_{y=x+1}^{N} fHD(C_{x}, C_{y})
</math>

where ''μ<sub>1</sub>'' is the intra-fHD mean, ''N'' is the number of repeated measurements, and ''C<sub>x</sub>'' and ''C<sub>y</sub>'' are arrays from the intra-device set {''C''}.

Reliability is then defined as:

<math>
Reliability = (1 - \mu_{1}) \times 100\%
</math>

Ideally, ''μ<sub>1</sub>'' would be 0, indicating that repeated measurements of the same PUF instance produce identical responses. In practice, however, achieving an intra-fHD mean of 0 is difficult for reasonably sized identifiers due to factors such as noise, alignment errors, and other environmental influences, which increase the observed intra-fHD.<ref name=":2" />

=== Uniformity ===
Uniformity quantifies the proportion of 0s and 1s in the binary output of a PUF, also referred to as the "[[Hamming weight]]" or "bias." A value of 0.5 (50%) indicates maximum entropy, with each output bit equally likely to be 0 or 1.

Mathematically, for a binary array {{math|D_n}} with {{math|a}} rows and {{math|b}} columns, where {{math|D_{n,I,J}}} denotes the value of the pixel at coordinates {{math|(I,J)}}, the uniformity of a single PUF response is defined as:

<math>
U_{n} = \frac{1}{a \cdot b} \sum_{I=1}^{a} \sum_{J=1}^{b} D_{n,I,J}
</math>

The overall uniformity for a set of {{math|N}} PUF responses is then:

<math>
U = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=1}^{N} U_{n}
</math>

Here, <math>U_n</math> is a number between 0 and 1 representing the average pixel value of the array. The set <math>\{D\}</math> is sometimes used to analyze uniformity across multiple devices.

=== Effective number of independent bits ===
The effective number of independent bits (ENIB) quantifies the amount of unique, uncorrelated information in a PUF response. High ENIB values indicate low redundancy and high entropy across the output.

It is defined mathematically as:

<math>
N = \frac{\mu_{2} (1 - \mu_{2})}{\sigma_{2}^{2}}
</math>

where <math>N</math> is the ENIB, <math>\mu_{2}</math> is the mean of the inter-fractional Hamming distance (inter-fHD) distribution, and <math>\sigma_{2}</math> is its standard deviation (with <math>\sigma_{2}^{2}</math> representing the variance).

In some literature, this metric is also referred to as the ''degrees of freedom'' (DoF) of the PUF response.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kim |first1=M. S. |last2=Lee |first2=G. J. |last3=Leem |first3=J. W. |last4=Choi |first4=S. |last5=Kim |first5=Y. L. |last6=Song |first6=Y. M. |year=2022 |title=Revisiting silk: A lens-free optical physical unclonable function |journal=Nature Communications |volume=13 |issue=1 |page=247 |bibcode=2022NatCo..13..247K |doi=10.1038/s41467-021-27278-5  |doi-access=free|pmc=8752800 |pmid=35017474}}</ref>

=== Decidability ===
Decidability measures how well a PUF can distinguish between different devices. Higher values indicate that the PUF responses are more reliably separable, while a value of zero means no distinguishable features exist, rendering the PUF ineffective.

It is defined mathematically as:

<math>
d' = \frac{|\mu_1 - \mu_2|}{\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2}{2}}}
</math>

where <math>d'</math> represents decidability, <math>\mu_{1}</math> is the mean of the intra-fractional Hamming distance (intra-fHD) distribution, <math>\mu_{2}</math> is the mean of the inter-fHD distribution, <math>\sigma_{1}</math> is the standard deviation of the intra-fHDs, and <math>\sigma_{2}</math> is the standard deviation of the inter-fHDs.
<ref>{{cite book |last=Daugman |first=J. |title=The Essential Guide to Image Processing |publisher=Elsevier |year=2009 |editor-last=Gonzalez |editor-first=R. |pages=715–739 |chapter=How iris recognition works |editor-last2=Woods |editor-first2=R.}}</ref>

==Error correction==
In many applications, it is important that the output is stable. If the PUF is used for a key in cryptographic algorithms, it is necessary that error correction be done to correct any errors caused by the underlying physical processes and reconstruct exactly the same key each time under all operating conditions. In principle there are two basic concepts: pre-processing and post-processing error correction code (ECC).<ref name="autogenerated2012"/>
<ref>C. Bohm, M. Hofer, and W. Pribyl, "A microcontroller SRAM-PUF," in Network and System Security (NSS), 2011 5th International Conference September 2011, pp. 269–273.</ref>

On-chip ECC units increase size, power, and data processing time overheads; they also expose vulnerabilities to power analysis attacks that attempt to model the PUF mathematically. Alternatively, some PUF designs like the EC-PUF do not require an on-chip ECC unit.<ref name="ieeexplore.ieee.org"/>

Strategies have been developed which lead SRAM PUF to become more reliable over time without degrading the other PUF quality measures such as security and efficiency.<ref>Maes, R, and Van der Leest, V. [https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/Countering-the-effects-of-silicon-aging-on-SRAM-PU-Maes-Leest/1f14804db49017328e96afe1de36c40cfb19556b "Countering the effects of silicon aging on SRAM PUFs"], Proceedings of the 2014 IEEE International Symposium on Hardware-Oriented Security and Trust (HOST)</ref>

Research at [[Carnegie Mellon University]] into various PUF implementations found that some error reduction techniques reduced errors in PUF response in a range of ~70 percent to ~100 percent.<ref>Bhargava, M. [https://kilthub.cmu.edu/articles/Reliable_Secure_Efficient_Physical_Unclonable_Functions/6721310 "Reliable, Secure, Efficient Physical Unclonable Functions"], Carnegie Mellon University Research Showcase @ CMU, Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, 2013</ref>

Research at the University of Massachusetts Amherst to improve the reliability of SRAM PUF-generated keys posited an error correction technique to reduce the error rate.<ref>Vijayakumar, A.; Patil, V.C.; and Kundu, S. [http://www.mdpi.com/2079-9268/7/1/2/htm "On Improving Reliability of SRAM-Based Physically Unclonable Functions"], Journal of Low Power Electronics and Applications, 12 January 2017</ref>

Joint reliability–secrecy coding methods based on [[transform coding]] are used to obtain significantly higher reliabilities for each bit generated from a PUF such that low-complexity error-correcting codes such as [[BCH codes]] suffice to satisfy a block error probability constraint of 1 bit errors out of 1 billion bits.<ref>Gunlu, O.; Kernetzky, T.; Iscan, O.; Sidorenko, V.; Kramer, G.; and Schaefer, R. [https://www.mdpi.com/1099-4300/20/5/340/htm "Secure and Reliable Key Agreement with Physical Unclonable Functions"], Entropy Journal, 3 May 2018</ref>

Nested [[Polar code (coding theory)|polar codes]] are used for [[vector quantization]] and error correction jointly. Their performance is asymptotically optimal in terms of, for a given blocklength, the maximum number of secret bits generated, the minimum amount of private information leaked about the PUF outputs, and minimum storage required. The fuzzy commitment scheme and fuzzy extractors are shown to be suboptimal in terms of the minimum storage.<ref name="gunluwz">Gunlu, O.; Iscan, O.; Sidorenko, V.; and Kramer, G. [https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.00275 "Code Constructions for Physical Unclonable Functions and Biometric Secrecy Systems"], IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security, 15 April 2019</ref>

==Availability==
* PUF technology can be licensed from several companies including [[eMemory]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.ememory.com.tw/ |title=Home |website=ememory.com.tw}}</ref> or its subsidiary, [[PUFsecurity]],<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pufsecurity.com/|title=PUFsecurity {{!}} Secure the Connected World {{!}} Taiwan|website=Pufsecurity|language=en|access-date=2019-12-17}}</ref> Enthentica,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.enthentica.com/|title=Enthentica Company Website|website=www.enthentica.com}}</ref> ICTK, Intrinsic ID,<ref name="IntrinsicID">[https://www.intrinsic-id.com Intrinsic ID company website]</ref> Invia, QuantumTrace, Granite Mountain Technologies,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Physically Unclonable Functions |url=https://gmt-semi.com/puf |access-date=2022-04-08 |website=Granite Mountain Technologies |language=en-US}}</ref> Secure-IC<ref>{{Cite web |title=Physically Unclonable Functions |url=https://www.secure-ic.com/products/securyzr/security-ip/key-management/puf-ip/ |access-date=2026-03-11 |website=Secure-IC |language=en-US}}</ref> and Verayo.
* PUF technology has been implemented in several hardware platforms including [[Microsemi]] SmartFusion2,<ref>[https://www.militaryaerospace.com/computers/article/16716318/microsemi-to-offer-intrinsicid-security-in-fpgas-and-systemsonchip-for-sensitive-military-applications Microsemi to offer Intrinsic-ID security in FPGAs and systems-on-chip for sensitive military applications], Military & Aerospace Electronics, August 2011</ref> [[NXP]] SmartMX2,<ref>[https://www.eetimes.com/document.asp?doc_id=1254886# NXP and Intrinsic-ID to raise smart chip security], EETimes, 2010</ref> Coherent Logix HyperX, InsideSecure MicroXsafe, [[Altera]] Stratix 10,<ref>[https://newsroom.intel.com/news-releases/altera-partners-intrinsic-id-develop-worlds-secure-high-end-fpga/#gs.0qyiip Altera Partners with Intrinsic-ID to Develop World's Most Secure High-End FPGA], October 12, 2015</ref> [[Redpine Signals]] WyzBee and Xilinx Zynq Ultrascale+.<ref>{{Cite press release | url=http://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases/verayo-puf-ip-on-xilinx-zynq-ultrascale-mpsoc-devices-addresses-security-demands-300357805.html | title=Verayo PUF IP on Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC Devices Addresses Security Demands}}</ref>

==Vulnerabilities==

In 2011, university research showed that delay-based PUF implementations are vulnerable to [[side-channel attack]]s<ref>{{citation | last1 = Merli | first1 = Dominik | last2 = Schuster | first2 = Dieter | last3 = Stumpf | first3 = Frederic | last4 = Sigl | first4 = Georg | title = Trust and Trustworthy Computing. 4th International Conference, TRUST 2011, Pittsburgh, PA, USA, June 22–24, 2011. Proceedings | date = 2011 | contribution = Side Channel Analysis of PUFs and Fuzzy Extractors | series  = Lecture Notes in Computer Science | volume  = 6740 | publisher = Springer Berlin Heidelberg| pages = 33–47 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-642-21599-5_3 | isbn = 978-3-642-21598-8| url = http://publica.fraunhofer.de/documents/N-174395.html | url-access = subscription }}</ref><ref>{{cite thesis | last = Schuster | first = Dieter | title = Side-Channel Analysis of Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) | type = Diploma | publisher = [[Technische Universität München]] | year = 2010 | url = http://www.sec.in.tum.de/assets/studentwork/finished/Schuster2010.pdf | access-date = 2013-06-28 | archive-date = 2015-07-09 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150709073049/https://www.sec.in.tum.de/assets/studentwork/finished/Schuster2010.pdf }}</ref> and recommends that countermeasures be employed in the design to prevent this type of attack. Also, improper implementation of PUF could introduce "[[Backdoor (computing)|backdoors]]" to an otherwise secure system.<ref>{{cite conference | last1 = Rührmair | first1 = Ulrich | last2 = van Dijk | first2 = Marten | title = PUFs in Security Protocols: Attack Models and Security Evaluations | conference = 2013 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy . May 19–22, 2013 San Francisco, CA, USA | year = 2013 | url = http://www.ieee-security.org/TC/SP2013/papers/4977a286.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{citation | last1 = Katzenbeisser | first1 = Stefan | last2 = Kocabas | first2 = Ünal | last3 = Rožic | first3 = Vladimir | last4 = Sadeghi | first4 = Ahmad-Reza | last5 = Verbauwhede | first5 = Ingrid | last6 = Wachsmann | first6 = Christian | title = Cryptographic Hardware and Embedded Systems – CHES 2012. 14th International Workshop, Leuven, Belgium, September 9–12, 2012. Proceedings | date = 2012 | contribution = PUFs: Myth, Fact or Busted? A Security Evaluation of Physically Unclonable Functions (PUFs) Cast in Silicon | series  = Lecture Notes in Computer Science | volume  = 7428 | publisher = Springer Berlin Heidelberg| pages = 283–301 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-642-33027-8_17 | isbn = 978-3-642-33026-1 | url = http://eprint.iacr.org/2012/557.pdf| doi-access = free }}</ref> In June 2012, Dominik Merli, a scientist at Fraunhofer Research Institution for Applied and Integrated Security (AISEC) further claimed that PUF introduces more entry points for hacking into a cryptographic system and that further investigation into the vulnerabilities of PUFs is required before PUFs can be used in practical security-related applications.<ref>{{cite conference | last = Merli | first = Dominik | title = Hardware Attacks on PUFs | conference = Proceedings AHS2012, NASA/ESA Conference on Adaptive Hardware and Systems. June 25 – 28, 2012 Erlangen, Germany. | year = 2012 | url = http://www.see.ed.ac.uk/ahs2012/Tutorial_4_Part2.pdf | access-date = 2013-06-28 | archive-date = 2015-06-10 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20150610230403/http://www.see.ed.ac.uk/ahs2012/Tutorial_4_Part2.pdf }}</ref>
The presented attacks are all on PUFs implemented in insecure systems, such as [[Field-programmable gate array|FPGA]] or static RAM (SRAM). It is also important to ensure that the environment is suitable for the needed security level,<ref name="autogenerated2012">{{cite book | last = Christoph | first = Boehm | title = Physical Unclonable Functions in Theory and Practice | publisher=Springer| year = 2012 }}</ref> as otherwise attacks taking advantage of temperature and other variations may be possible.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Anagnostopoulos|first1=N.A.|last2=Arul |first2=T. |last3=Rosenstihl|first3=M.|last4=Schaller|first4=A.|last5=Gabmeyer|first5=S.|last6=Katzenbeisser|first6=S. |year=2019 |title=Attacking SRAM PUFs using very-low-temperature data remanence |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0141933118305076 |journal=Microprocessors and Microsystems |volume=71 |article-number=102864|doi=10.1016/j.micpro.2019.102864| editor1-last=Kitsos| editor1-first=P.|publisher=Elsevier|s2cid=201138643|issn=0141-9331|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

In 2015, some studies claimed it is possible to attack certain kinds of PUFs with low-cost equipment in a matter of milliseconds. A team at Ruhr Universität of Bochum, Germany, demonstrated a method to create a model of XOR arbiter PUFs and thus be able to predict their response to any kind of challenge. Their method requires only 4 CRPs, which even on resource-constrained devices should not take more than about 200ms to produce. Using this method and a $25 device or an NFC-enabled smartphone, the team was able to successfully clone PUF-based RFID cards stored in the wallet of users while it was in their back pocket.<ref name=":0">{{cite conference | last1 = Becker | first1 = Georg | title = Cryptographic Hardware and Embedded Systems -- CHES 2015 | chapter = The Gap Between Promise and Reality: On the Insecurity of XOR Arbiter PUFs | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science | conference = Lecture Notes in Computer Science | year = 2015 | volume = 9293 | pages = 535–555 | doi = 10.1007/978-3-662-48324-4_27 | isbn = 978-3-662-48323-7 | doi-access = free }}</ref>

=== Provable machine learning attacks ===
The attacks mentioned above range from invasive, e.g.,<ref name="nedos2013">{{cite conference | last1 = Helfmeier | first1 = Clemens | last2 = Nedospasov | first2 = Dmitry | last3 = Boit | first3 = Christian | last4 = Seifert | first4 = Jean-Pierre | title = Cloning Physically Unclonable Functions | conference = IEEE Hardware Oriented Security and Trust (IEEE HOST 2013). June 2–3, 2013 Austin, TX, USA | year = 2013 | url = http://users.sec.t-labs.tu-berlin.de/~nedos/host2013.pdf | access-date = 2014-09-11 | archive-date = 2016-08-01 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20160801032523/http://users.sec.t-labs.tu-berlin.de/~nedos/host2013.pdf }}</ref> to non-invasive attacks.<ref name=":0" /> One of the most celebrated types of non-invasive attacks is [[machine learning]] (ML) attacks.<ref name=":0" /> From the beginning of the era of PUFs, it has been doubted if these primitives are subject to this type of attacks.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Gassend|first1=Blaise|last2=Clarke|first2=Dwaine|last3=van Dijk|first3=Marten|last4=Devadas|first4=Srinivas|title=Proceedings of the 9th ACM conference on Computer and communications security |chapter=Silicon physical random functions |date=2002|pages=148–160 |location=New York, New York, USA|publisher=ACM Press|doi=10.1145/586110.586132|isbn=978-1-58113-612-8|s2cid=1788365}}</ref> In the lack of thorough analysis and mathematical proofs of the security of PUFs, ad hoc attacks against PUFs have been introduced in the literature. Consequently, countermeasures presented to cope with these attacks are less effective. In line with these efforts, it has been conjectured if PUFs can be considered as circuits, being provably hard to break.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Herder|first1=Charles|last2=Ren|first2=Ling|last3=van Dijk|first3=Marten|last4=Yu|first4=Meng-Day|last5=Devadas|first5=Srinivas|date=2017-01-01|title=Trapdoor computational fuzzy extractors and stateless cryptographically-secure physical unclonable functions|journal=IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing|volume=14|issue=1|pages=65–82|doi=10.1109/tdsc.2016.2536609|bibcode=2017ITDSC..14...65H |issn=1545-5971|doi-access=free}}</ref> In response, a mathematical framework has been suggested, where provable ML algorithms against several known families of PUFs have been introduced.<ref>{{Cite book|title=On the learnability of physically unclonable functions|last=Ganji|first=Fatemeh|publisher=Springer|year=2018|isbn=978-3-319-76716-1}}</ref>

Along with this provable ML framework, to assess the security of PUFs against ML attacks, property testing algorithms have been reintroduced in the hardware security community and made publicly accessible.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://trust-hub.org/resource/software/PUFmeter_version_00.pdf|title=PUFmeter: A Property Testing Tool for Physically Unclonable Functions|last=Ganji|first=Fatemeh|date=2018}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://trust-hub.org/software|title=Software Developed for the Trust-Hub Project (Available for Download)|date=2018}}</ref> These algorithms trace their roots back to well-established fields of research, namely [[property testing]], [[machine learning theory]], and [[Boolean analysis]].

ML attacks can also apply to PUFs because most of the pre and post-processing methods applied until now ignore the effect of correlations between PUF-circuit outputs. For instance, obtaining one bit by comparing two ring oscillator outputs is a method to decrease the correlation. However, this method does not remove all correlations. Therefore, the classic transforms from the signal-processing literature are applied to raw PUF-circuit outputs to decorrelate them before quantizing the outputs in the transform domain to generate bit sequences. Such decorrelation methods can help to overcome the correlation-based information leakages about the PUF outputs even if the ambient temperature and supply voltage change.<ref>Gunlu, O.; Iscan, O.; and Kramer, G. [https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/7368554 "Reliable secret key generation from physical unclonable functions under varying environmental conditions"], IEEE Workshop on Information Forensics and Security, 4 January 2016</ref>

== Optical PUFs ==
Optical physically unclonable functions (OPUFs or O-PUFs) rely on a random optical multiple-scattering medium, which serves as a token.<ref name=":1" /> Optical PUFs offer a promising approach to developing entity authentication schemes that are robust against many of the aforementioned attacks. However, their security against emulation attacks can be ensured only in the case of quantum readout (see below), or when the database of challenge-response pairs is somehow encrypted.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Nikolopoulos|first=Georgios M.|date=July 2021|title=Remote Quantum-Safe Authentication of Entities with Physical Unclonable Functions|journal=Photonics|language=en|volume=8|issue=7|page=289|doi=10.3390/photonics8070289|arxiv=2108.00468|bibcode=2021Photo...8..289N |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Optical PUFs can be made very easily: a varnish containing glitter, a metallic paint, or a frosted finish obtained by sandblasting a surface, for example, are practically impossible to clone. Their appearance changes depending on the point of view and the lighting. Authentication of an optical PUF requires a photographic acquisition. This could be to measure the luminosity of several of its parts. Acquisitions are then compared to a database ID which is produced in the 'registration' stage. This acquisition can be supplemented by an additional acquisition either from another point of view, or under different lighting to verify that this results in a modification of the appearance of the PUF.
 
Recent research has investigated methods to improve the robustness and longevity of optical PUFs under varying environmental conditions. One such approach involves the binarisation of optically acquired inputs to reduce the impact of noise and glare, thereby increasing the consistency of authentication results over time.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Longmate |first1=Kieran D. |last2=Abdelazim |first2=Nema M. |last3=Ball |first3=Elliott M. |last4=Majaniemi |first4=Joonas |last5=Young |first5=Robert J. |title=Improving the longevity of optically-read quantum dot physical unclonable functions |journal=Scientific Reports |volume=11 |issue=1 |page=10999 |year=2021 |doi=10.1038/s41598-021-90129-2 |doi-access=free|pmid=34040030 |pmc=8155066 |bibcode=2021NatSR..1110999L }}</ref>

A variety of figures of merit—such as uniqueness, reliability, and randomness—can be used to evaluate optical PUFs; however, because most electronic PUFs (E-PUFs) are independent and identically distributed (IID), their metrics tend to rely on mean-based assumptions. Optical PUFs often violate these assumptions, so care must be taken when interpreting metrics like reliability. A Python-based toolkit, <code>pyopticalpuf</code>, has been developed to facilitate more standardised and reproducible evaluation of optically imaged PUFs, and is publicly available on [[GitHub]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=pyopticalpuf |url=https://github.com/ellaandr/pyopticalpuf |website=GitHub |access-date=2025-07-25}}</ref>

This can be done with a smartphone, without additional equipment, using optical means to determine the position in which the smartphone is in relation to the PUF.

Theoretical investigations suggest that optical PUFs with nonlinear multiple-scattering media, may be more robust  than their linear counterparts against the potential cloning of the medium.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Nikolopoulos |first=Georgios M. |date=2022 |title=Effects of Kerr Nonlinearity in Physical Unclonable Functions |journal=Applied Sciences |language=en |volume=12 |issue=23 |article-number=11985 |doi=10.3390/app122311985 |issn=2076-3417|doi-access=free |arxiv=2211.11499 }}</ref>

=== O-PUF history ===
The development of optical physical unclonable functions began with the doctoral thesis of Ravi Pappu at MIT in 2001, followed by the seminal 2002 ''Science'' publication that introduced volumetric scattering from a laser as a basis for optical unclonable responses.<ref>Pappu, R. (2001). ''Physical one-way functions,'' PhD thesis, Massachusetts Institute of Technology.</ref><ref>Pappu, R.; Recht, B.; Taylor, J.; Gershenfeld, N. (2002). "Physical one-way functions". ''Science''. 297 (5589): 2026–2030.</ref> As the field emerged, Blaise Gassend's 2002 MIT master's thesis described silicon-based physical random functions, establishing an immediate break-away of the field into the first of many different kinds of PUF.<ref>Gassend, B. (2002). ''Physical Random Functions, Master's''. MIT.</ref> This initial work laid the groundwork for the field and established key concepts like the challenge-response pair.

Building on the O-PUF work, researchers at Philips Research Laboratories in the Netherlands contributed important theoretical advances: Tuyls et al (2004)<ref>Tuyls, P.; Skoric, B.; Akkermans, T.; Ophey, W.; Stallinga, S. (2004). "Security analysis of physical uncloneable functions". In ''Symposium On Information Theory''.</ref> presented a security analysis of PUFs, Ignatenko et al. (2006)<ref>Ignatenko, T.; Schrijen, G.-J.; Skoric, B.; Tuyls, P.; Willems, F. (2006). "Estimating the secrecy-rate of physical unclonable functions with the context-tree weighting method". In ''2006 IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory'', pp. 499–503. IEEE.</ref> developed methods for estimating security rates, and Kursawe et al. (2009) introduced the idea of reconfigurable PUFs for tamper-proof storage.<ref>Kursawe, K.; Sadeghi, A.-R.; Schellekens, D.; Skoric, B.; Tuyls, P. (2009). "Reconfigurable physical unclonable functions–enabling technology for tamper-resistant storage". In ''2009 IEEE International Workshop on Hardware-Oriented Security and Trust'', pp. 22–29. IEEE.</ref>

Later, Rührmair et al at [[LMU Munich]] reinvigorated the field with works such as ''Optical PUFs Reloaded'' (2013) and the comprehensive review ''PUFs at a Glance'' (2014) which worked on the key definitions for the field.<ref>Rührmair, U.; Hilgers, C.; Urban, S.; Weiershäuser, A.; Dinter, E.; Forster, B.; Jirauschek, C. (2013). "Optical PUFs Reloaded". ''Cryptology ePrint Archive''.</ref><ref>Rührmair, U.; Holcomb, D. E. (2014). "PUFs at a Glance". In ''2014 Design, Automation & Test in Europe Conference & Exhibition (DATE)'', pp. 1–6. IEEE.</ref> A second wave of optical implementations followed: Cao et al. (2017) demonstrated identification using imperfections in two-dimensional materials, Mesaritakis et al. (2018) proposed a multimode optical waveguide PUF, Kim et al. (2022) revisited silk-based substrates for lens-free O-PUFs, Nocentini et al. (2024) reported all-optical multilevel PUF architectures and many other papers helped diversify the field.<ref>Cao, Y.; Robson, A. J.; Alharbi, A.; Roberts, J.; Woodhead, C. S.; Noori, Y. J.; Bernardo-Gavito, R.; Shahrjerdi, D.; Roedig, U.; Fal'ko, V. I.; et al. (2017). "Optical identification using imperfections in 2D materials". ''2D Materials''. 4(4): 045021.</ref><ref>Mesaritakis, C.; Akriotou, M.; Kapsalis, A.; Grivas, E.; Chaintoutis, C.; Nikas, T.; Syvridis, D. (2018). "Physical unclonable function based on a multi-mode optical waveguide". ''Scientific Reports''. 8(1): 9653.</ref><ref>Kim, M. S.; Lee, G. J.; Leem, J. W.; Choi, S.; Kim, Y. L.; Song, Y. M. (2022). "Revisiting silk: a lens-free optical physical unclonable function". ''Nature Communications''. 13(1): 247.</ref><ref>Nocentini, S.; Rührmair, U.; Barni, M.; Wiersma, D. S.; Riboli, F. (2024). "All-optical multilevel physical unclonable functions". ''Nature Materials''. 23(3): 369–376.</ref>

Together, these trace the progression of O-PUFs from early scattering-based prototypes to a diverse family of optical identification technologies. While the field started with laser-based security generation, the more recent work signals a diversification to O-PUFs based on a wide range of material properties from polarisation to nano materials. Additionally the iteration of smartphone technology has provided a new area for expansion in the field, with work on the consumer accessible O-PUFs for authentication.<ref>Ali, S. R.; Kershaw, S. V.; Faisal, M. M.; Halak, B.; Abdelazim, N. M. (2025). "Illuminating Advances in Materials: Optical Physical Unclonable Functions for Security Applications". ''Advanced Optical Materials''. e01564. Wiley Online Library.</ref>

== Chemical unclonable function ==
Chemical unclonable functions (CUFs) are analogous to physical unclonable functions but are based on chemical reactions. As of May 2026 only one type of CUF has been presented, a DNA-based function by Luescher et al.<ref name=":03">{{Cite journal |last1=Luescher|first1=Anne M.|last2=Gimpel|first2=Andreas L.|last3=Stark|first3=Wendelin J.|last4=Heckel|first4=Reinhard|last5=Grass|first5=Robert N.|date=2024-04-05|title=Chemical unclonable functions based on operable random DNA pools|journal=Nature Communications|language=en|volume=15|issue=1|article-number=2955 |doi=10.1038/s41467-024-47187-7 |doi-access=free|issn=2041-1723|pmc=10997750|pmid=38580696 |bibcode=2024NatCo..15.2955L }}</ref> This CUF is based on pools of partially random DNA molecules that produce a consistent output (DNA sequence reads) when presented with an input (performing [[Polymerase chain reaction|PCR]] with specific [[Primer (molecular biology)|primers]]). Due to chemical modifications applied to the ends of the molecules, the DNA pool is neither clonable nor able to be sequenced, and even given perfect knowledge about the sequences comprising the pool it would not be feasible to re-synthesize it given the number of unique sequences (100 million in the current implementation). Thus reverse-engineering is not realistically possible.<ref name=":03"/>

Proposed applications include authentication of art works and anti-counterfeit tagging of medications by applying the DNA pools to the individual doses of medications themselves.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Luescher|first1=Anne M.|last2=Stark|first2=Wendelin J.|last3=Grass|first3=Robert N.|date=2024-11-05|title=DNA-Based Chemical Unclonable Functions for Cryptographic Anticounterfeit Tagging of Pharmaceuticals|journal=ACS Nano|language=en|volume=18|issue=44|pages=30774–30785|doi=10.1021/acsnano.4c10870|issn=1936-0851|pmc=11544705|pmid=39438327 |bibcode=2024ACSNa..1830774L }}</ref> Since the verification of the sample requires laboratory equipment and takes several hours to complete, the DNA-pool based CUF is not currently applicable to time-sensitive areas like digital encryption.<ref>{{Cite web |last=online|first=heise|date=2025-12-30|title=39C3: When Molecules Become Cryptographic Functions|url=https://www.heise.de/en/news/39C3-When-Molecules-Become-Cryptographic-Functions-11126533.html|access-date=2026-04-13|website=heise online|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-04-08|title=Protecting art and passwords with biochemistry|url=https://ethz.ch/en/news-and-events/eth-news/news/2024/04/protecting-art-and-passwords-with-biochemistry.html|access-date=2026-04-13|website=ETH Zurich|language=en}}</ref>

== Twin PUFs ==
Physically correlated pairs of PUFs, commonly referred to as ''twin PUFs'', have been demonstrated in different physical platforms, including carbon nanotube (CNT)-based electronic PUFs<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zhong |first1=Donglai |last2=Liu |first2=Jingxia |last3=Xiao |first3=Mengmeng |last4=Xie |first4=Yunong |last5=Shi |first5=Huiwen |last6=Liu |first6=Lijun |last7=Zhao |first7=Chenyi |last8=Ding |first8=Li |last9=Peng |first9=Lian-Mao |last10=Zhang |first10=Zhiyong |date=July 2022 |title=Twin physically unclonable functions based on aligned carbon nanotube arrays |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41928-022-00787-x |journal=Nature Electronics |language=en |volume=5 |issue=7 |pages=424–432 |doi=10.1038/s41928-022-00787-x |issn=2520-1131|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and optical scattering PUFs.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Marakis |first1=E. |title=Clones of the Unclonable: Nanoduplicating Optical PUFs and Applications |date=2022-12-23 |url=http://arxiv.org/abs/2212.12495 |access-date=2026-07-13 |arxiv=2212.12495 |last2=Rührmair |first2=U. |last3=Lachner |first3=M. |last4=Uppu |first4=R. |last5=Škorić |first5=B. |last6=Pinkse |first6=P. W. H.}}</ref> Such correlated PUF pairs enable two devices to generate highly correlated responses, which can be converted into a common cryptographic key using information reconciliation and privacy amplification.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Nikolopoulos |first=Georgios M |date=2026-07-01 |title=Noise-limited secret key agreement with twin optical physically unclonable functions |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/2040-8986/ae81c2 |journal=Journal of Optics |volume=28 |issue=7 |page=075702 |doi=10.1088/2040-8986/ae81c2 |arxiv=2607.04936 |bibcode=2026JOpt...28g5702N |issn=2040-8978}}</ref> Twin optical PUFs can be integrated into quantum key distribution networks, as a mechanism for establishing an initial pre-shared secret key between two honest users, without relying on computational assumptions or trusted third parties.
